chapters.title: Chapter 5: Running a Clean Cap Table in India

lessons.title: Cap Table Mistakes That Break Due Diligence

children.text: Diligence is not an exam you pass or fail. It is a list of problems, and every problem on that list turns into one of three things: a delay, a reduction in price, or an indemnity you personally sign. Founders who understand that stop treating diligence as an inspection to survive and start treating it as a negotiation they can prepare for months in advance.

body.text: Every line on your cap table that you cannot explain in one sentence, with a document attached, will cost you money. Find those lines before the investor's lawyer does.

children.text: The Nine Findings That Come Up Again and Again

body.caption: Common cap table findings, their cost and their fix

cells: Dead equity
A departed co-founder still holds a large stake with no vesting
Investors discount the team, or demand a buyback before closing
Negotiate a buyback or partial surrender early, and document it
No founder vesting
Nothing in the founders' agreement or the articles
A condition precedent requiring fresh vesting on the investor's terms
Put vesting in place yourself, before the term sheet
Undocumented promises
An employee or advisor says they were promised a percentage
Contingent liability, escrow or an indemnity from the founders
Convert every promise into a formal grant, or settle it in writing
Missing convertibles
A note or iSAFE that is not on the fully diluted cap table
Recalculated dilution mid-deal, and lost trust
List every instrument with the shares it produces at the expected price
Grants outside the plan
Options granted with no board-approved plan, or beyond the pool size
Grants may be invalid, requiring ratification and a pool increase
Approve a proper plan, ratify past grants, keep an option register
Records that do not reconcile
Share counts differ between the cap table, the register of members and MCA filings
Weeks of remediation and fees, sometimes a compounding application
Reconcile quarterly, as covered in the previous lesson
Shares in someone else's name
Shares held by a relative or employee for a founder's benefit
A serious legal exposure that can stop a deal outright
Never do this. If it exists, take legal advice immediately
Money received without allotment
Share application money sitting on the balance sheet for months
Breach of the allotment timelines, with refund and interest exposure
Allot within the prescribed period or refund on time
Unreported foreign investment
A non-resident cheque with no FEMA filing
Penalties and a compounding process that can delay closing
File on time, and check reporting before accepting foreign money

body.text: Never fix a documentation gap by backdating. Signing a resolution today and dating it two years ago turns a compliance problem into a much more serious one, exposes everyone who signs it, and is exactly the kind of thing that surfaces when a disgruntled ex-employee talks to an investor's lawyer. Regularise with the correct current date and disclose the delay.

children.text: The Same Company, Two Ways to Arrive at Diligence

body.title: Found by you, or found by them

columns.label: You found it first
points: Disclosed in your own words, with a remediation plan and dates
Priced once, as a known item
You control the timetable and the professionals involved
Signals a team that runs a tight company

columns.label: Their lawyer found it
points: Disclosed in a diligence report you did not write
Priced twice: the problem itself, and the doubt about what else is hidden
Their timetable, their counsel, your cost
Triggers a wider review of everything else

body.text: Use the disclosure schedule deliberately. It is the annexure to the investment agreement where you list exceptions to the warranties you are giving. Anything properly disclosed there is something the investor has accepted with their eyes open, and it usually cannot be claimed against later. Anything you leave out because it felt small is exactly what an indemnity claim is built on.

children.text: What a Clean-Up Actually Looks Like

Six months before raising its Series C, TiffinBox runs its own diligence. Meera hires a company secretary and a lawyer to review the company as though they worked for the investor. They find three things.

events.title: An advisor with an undocumented promise
events.description: An early advisor was told he would get 0.5% and never received a grant letter. Resolution: a formal option grant for an agreed number of options, vesting already complete, with a written confirmation that this settles all claims.

events.title: Option grants ahead of the pool
events.description: Grants totalling more than the approved pool were issued after a strong hiring quarter. Resolution: the board approves a pool increase and ratifies the excess grants, and the option register is rebuilt from grant letters.

events.title: Certificates never issued
events.description: Share certificates for one allotment were never issued and stamp duty was unpaid. Resolution: certificates issued with duty paid, the register of members corrected, and a note prepared for the disclosure schedule.

events.title: A four-page diligence response
events.description: When the Series C investor's list arrives, every answer already exists in one folder, with one dated cap table that reconciles to the register and the MCA record.

stats.label: Typical clean-up window
stats.context: Before you start meeting investors, not during the round

stats.label: Common delay when found late
stats.context: Exactly when your runway is shortest

stats.label: What it usually costs
stats.context: Far cheaper than a price chip or a founder indemnity

stats.label: Documents to keep ready
stats.context: Reconciled to the register of members and the last annual return

body.label: Who carries the risk
body.context: Investment agreements typically include founder warranties and indemnities on share capital and title to shares. An unresolved equity promise or a defective allotment is not just a company problem. It can be a claim against you, sometimes for years after closing.

body.title: The cap table that understates itself
body.prompt: A founder's cap table shows 24,000 fully diluted shares, and she holds 9,000 of them. Diligence finds 300 granted options that were never recorded and a convertible note that will produce 800 shares. What is her actual fully diluted stake, to two decimal places?
body.explanation: True fully diluted shares = 24,000 + 300 + 800 = 25,100. Her stake is 9,000 ÷ 25,100 = 35.86%, not the 37.50% her spreadsheet showed. A 1.64 point error found by someone else is a credibility problem as much as an arithmetic one.

body.title: Name the annexure
body.textWithBlank: The annexure to an investment agreement where founders list known exceptions to the warranties they are giving is called the ___ schedule.
body.explanation: Properly disclosing a problem in the disclosure schedule generally prevents a claim on it later. Leaving it out because it seemed minor is how indemnity claims begin.

body.title: Which finding worries an investor most?
body.question: Four issues turn up in diligence on a Series A company. Which is most likely to stop the deal rather than merely delay or reprice it?
options: A PAS-3 filed 40 days late two years ago
Share certificates never issued for one allotment
A block of shares held in a founder's cousin's name for the founder's benefit, with no documentation
An option register that has not been updated for two quarters
body.explanation: The first, second and fourth are administrative and fixable: pay the additional fees, issue the certificates, rebuild the register. Shares held by one person for another's benefit with no documentation raises serious legal questions about who actually owns the company, and many investors will simply walk rather than price it.

body.title: Six weeks to close, four problems
body.scenario: Your Series B term sheet is signed with a six-week timetable. Diligence turns up four items: a co-founder who left three years ago holds 14% with no vesting or buyback right; an ex-employee claims she was promised 1% verbally and has an email from you saying "yes, roughly a percent, we'll paper it"; option grants exceed the board-approved pool by 400 options; and one allotment from 2023 has no share certificates issued. You have five months of runway.
body.prompt: How do you triage these, and what do you tell the investor?
body.modelAnswer:
Triage by what can stop the deal, not by what is easiest.

1. The ex-employee's claim is the most urgent, because you have written evidence supporting it. Approach her directly and settle it: a documented option grant of an agreed size, or a cash settlement, in exchange for a written full and final settlement. Do this yourself rather than letting it become a warranty negotiation. Left open, it becomes an indemnity you personally carry.
2. The dead equity is the item the investor cares most about strategically. You cannot force a buyback if there is no contractual right, so this is a commercial negotiation with the departed co-founder. Options include a partial buyback at an agreed price, funded from the round or by the investor, or a voluntary surrender of part of the stake in exchange for a clean settlement of any claims. Start the conversation on day one of the six weeks, because it is the one with the longest tail.
3. The excess option grants are fixable in a board meeting: approve a pool increase, ratify the grants, rebuild the option register from grant letters. Confirm the pool increase is reflected in the round's fully diluted numbers so the investor's percentage is not quietly recalculated at closing.
4. The missing certificates are the smallest item. Issue them with stamp duty paid, correct the register, and note the delay.

What to tell the investor: all four, in writing, this week, with an owner and a target date against each. Ask for the two administrative items to be closing deliverables rather than conditions precedent, and expect the ex-employee claim and the dead equity to be conditions precedent, which is reasonable.

The runway point matters: five months against a six-week timetable means you have some room but not much. Do not let the dead equity negotiation drift, because a departed co-founder who senses urgency will price it accordingly.

body.title: Run diligence on yourself first
steps: Reconcile the cap table against the register of members and the last annual return.
List every equity promise ever made, including verbal ones, and confirm each is either documented or settled.
Check that every option grant sits inside a board-approved plan and within the pool.
List every convertible with its cap, discount and expected share count.
Confirm founder vesting and leaver provisions exist and are in the articles, not only in a side agreement.
Confirm every allotment has resolutions, a filed PAS-3 and certificates issued with stamp duty paid.
Confirm every transfer has a Form SH-4 and a register entry, and that no shares are held by one person for another.
Confirm all foreign investment reporting has been filed.
Write your own disclosure schedule before anyone asks for it, with a fix and a date against each item.

cards.definition: The investor's review of a company's legal, financial and commercial position before investing.
The annexure listing exceptions to the warranties, protecting founders from claims on anything properly disclosed.
Something that must be completed before the investment closes and the money is released.
A statement of fact given by the company and founders in the investment agreement, which can be claimed against if untrue.
A promise to compensate the investor for a specified loss, often given personally by founders.
A board or shareholder approval given after the event to validate something already done.
A significant stake held by someone no longer contributing to the company.
A written agreement closing out all claims a person may have, used to resolve undocumented equity promises.

points: Diligence findings become delays, price reductions or indemnities, so treat them as negotiable items you can prepare for.

The recurring findings are dead equity, missing founder vesting, undocumented promises, missing convertibles, grants outside the pool, records that do not reconcile, shares held in another person's name, money received without allotment, and unreported foreign investment.
Never backdate documents. Regularise with the correct date and disclose the delay.
A problem you disclose is priced once. A problem they find is priced twice, because it raises doubt about everything else.
Use the disclosure schedule properly, since anything disclosed there generally cannot be claimed against later.
Founder warranties and indemnities mean these risks often sit with you personally, not just with the company.
Run your own diligence three to six months before you raise, and arrive with one dated cap table that reconciles to the register and the MCA record.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. TiffinBox Foods and the other companies and people described are fictional, and the timelines and costs given are general observations rather than benchmarks. How any particular finding is treated depends on the documents, the facts and the investor, and remedies such as ratification, compounding and settlements have their own legal requirements. Work with a qualified lawyer, company secretary and chartered accountant on any diligence clean-up or disclosure schedule.
